title: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (2 of 7)
hook: the self has four quarters, and the first is the waking world
tomorrow: Mandukya Upanishad (12 verses, one week): the four states; om, letter by letter (3 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Upanishad began: om, this syllable is all this. Past, present, future, and beyond. Did you let one silence last a little longer? Day two hundred fifty-four.

Every day you live in three different worlds, and you almost never think about it. In the morning you're here: coffee, emails, the bus. At night you're somewhere else entirely, flying, falling, late for an exam you never signed up for. And then, for a stretch, you're nowhere at all: deep, dreamless sleep, when there's no world and no you, and you wake up saying, I slept well. The Mandukya's second move is to take those three worlds seriously. It starts with the one you're in right now.
screen: `THREE WORLDS A DAY.` → `HERE, THERE, NOWHERE.` → `THE ONE YOU'RE IN NOW.`

segments.voice: Verse two: all this is Brahman. This self, atman, is Brahman. And this self has four quarters. Catushpat: four feet, the way a cow has four feet, or a coin was split into four quarters. Notice how bold that second sentence is. Ayam atma brahma: this self is Brahman. It's one of four famous great sayings in the Upanishads, the mahavakyas, and this is where it lives. The self you are and the ground of everything are the same, the Mandukya says, and then it maps that self in four parts. Verse three gives the first quarter. Its name is vaishvanara, the universal person, the one common to all people. Its field is the waking state. It knows outward: its attention faces the world. It has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, the text says; commentators explain the mouths as the senses, the organs of action, the breaths, and the inner faculties, all the ways we take the world in. And it enjoys the gross: solid things, things you can touch and count. That's you, reading this, hearing this. The waking self. It's the first quarter, and the Mandukya maps it to the first sound of om: a, the open mouth. We'll get to the sounds on day six. Why start here? Because it's where you already are. The Mandukya doesn't say waking life is fake, or bad. It says it's one quarter. Real, full, and not the whole of you.
screen: `THIS SELF IS BRAHMAN.` · `FOUR QUARTERS.` · `THE FIRST: THE WAKING STATE.` · `KNOWING OUTWARD, ENJOYING THE GROSS.` · then, large: `ONE QUARTER, NOT THE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Be fully in the waking state. Feel your weight on the chair. Hear the sounds around you. Feel the air on your skin, the taste in your mouth. This is the first quarter, knowing outward. Take it in with all nineteen mouths, as the text says. Then, gently, notice that you're aware of all of it: that the waking world is appearing to you. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The self is Brahman, and it has four quarters. The first is vaishvanara: the waking state, knowing outward.
Your line: the fourth. Today, three times, stop and notice: I'm awake, and this is the waking world. One quarter. Day two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: 'Ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2) is taught in Hindu Vedanta as one of four mahavakyas, great sayings, each drawn from a different Veda.

fork.setup: you're mapping the self in four parts. where do you start?
options: with the waking state, where the listener already is.
fork.reveal: the Mandukya starts with vaishvanara, the waking state: knowing outward, enjoying the gross.

original.note: Sanskrit: vaishvanara, common to all people, universal; the name of the waking self in Mandukya 3.

trapdoor: what you thought: the self is just the waking me.
what it means: the Mandukya says waking is one quarter of a four-part self.
what a scholar hears: Mandukya 3's 'seven limbs and nineteen mouths' draws on Chandogya 5.18; Shankara lists the nineteen as 5 senses, 5 organs of action, 5 breaths, mind, intellect, ego and citta.
